nameStory: The strawberry root weevil earned its name from its strong preference for strawberry plants, which make up a large portion of its diet. While it will munch on other plants when strawberries aren't available, this little beetle has such a sweet tooth for berry crops that farmers consider it one of their major strawberry pests. The 'root' part of its name comes from the fact that its larvae live underground, feeding on plant roots rather than leaves.
description: The strawberry root weevil is a small, dark-colored beetle with the characteristic long snout that gives all weevils their distinctive appearance. Like other weevils, it has a hard, oval-shaped body and elbowed antennae that look like tiny clubs at the tips. These beetles are flightless, so they get around by walking and can often be found slowly crawling on or near their favorite plants. They're small enough that you might mistake them for a piece of dark bark or soil at first glance.

idTips.label: Distinctive snout
idTips.description: Look for the long, curved snout (called a rostrum) extending from the head - it feels hard when touched and has the antennae attached partway down its length, giving it a distinctly 'beaky' appearance

idTips.label: Flightless movement
idTips.description: These beetles cannot fly and move with a slow, deliberate crawl - if disturbed, they'll often 'play dead' by tucking their legs under and dropping to the ground

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body appears dark brown to black with a slightly textured, matte surface that feels rough like fine sandpaper when gently touched

idTips.label: Elbowed antennae
idTips.description: Antennae bend at sharp angles like tiny elbows and end in small club-like tips that you can see clearly with a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Oval body shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly oval and somewhat flattened, with a hard shell that makes a tiny clicking sound if tapped gently with a fingernail

habitat: Look for strawberry root weevils in gardens, berry patches, and nurseries throughout New England, especially around strawberry plants, roses, and other cultivated ornamentals. They prefer areas with rich, moist soil where their larvae can develop in plant roots. You'll also find them in forest edges and disturbed areas where their wild host plants grow.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from soil and become active, beginning to feed on tender new growth. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on plants during warm days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are feeding heavily and laying eggs in the soil. Look for them at dusk or use a flashlight at night when they're most active.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding until cold weather arrives, preparing for winter dormancy. Late-season damage to plants may be most noticeable now.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil, leaf litter, or other protected spots and are generally not visible or active during cold months.

funFact: Despite being called the 'strawberry' root weevil, these beetles are actually flightless and can only reach new strawberry patches by walking there - which means infestations spread slowly but steadily outward like a tiny beetle invasion, one garden bed at a time!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its larger cousin, the black vine weevil, but strawberry root weevils are noticeably smaller and tend to stick closer to low-growing plants like strawberries rather than climbing up shrubs and trees. Remember: 'small and low' for strawberry weevils, 'big and high' for vine weevils.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while strawberries are their favorite, these weevils will happily munch on roses, rhododendrons, and many other garden plants. The species was first scientifically described by Carl Linnaeus way back in 1758, making it one of the earlier insects to be formally catalogued by science.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the black vine weevil, the strawberry root weevil is smaller and tends to stay closer to ground level rather than climbing up into shrubs and trees. Both are flightless and dark-colored with prominent snouts, but black vine weevils are noticeably larger and cause more damage to woody ornamental plants. If you find small weevils on your strawberry plants, they're likely this species; if you find larger ones munching on your rhododendrons, you're probably looking at black vine weevils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black vine weevils are larger and much darker than their close relative, the strawberry root weevil, which is smaller and more brownish in color.
